awd_titl_txt: SBIR Phase I:  AI-Enhanced Feedback to Accelerate Literacy, Creativity, and Student Engagement
awd_abstract_narration:
The broader/commercial impact of this Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project will significantly improve student literacy and creativity skills through our AI powered feedback system for creativity and ultimately prepare our students in the US for future job challenges. Inspire Reading will transform English language learning experience for students in grades 3-8, leading to greater impact on students' reading and writing skills. There are hundreds of products in the market but none of them have addressed the poor reading and writing outcomes we are seeing through national testing like NAEP with only 33% of students being proficient in 4th grade.  Through providing immediate AI-powered feedback on reading comprehension, writing and creativity skills, Inspire Reading will help prepare students for future challenges and the workforce. Positioned at the intersection of educational technology, cognitive science, and AI-driven assessment, Inspire Reading targets the $8 billion reading intervention market. By year three we aim to reach 500,000 students. The AI Feedback for Creativity (AIFC) auto feedback system, alignment to state standards, and focus on creativity provide a durable competitive advantage, making it a key driver of commercial success in the fast-growing AI-powered learning market with the goal of improving literacy for the two-thirds of the nation's 4th- and 8th-grade students scoring below levels of proficiency. 

This Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project centers on the development of an AI-powered feedback system for creativity (AIFC) designed to enhance literacy and creative thinking skills within the context of ELA learning. This addresses the pressing need for improved reading and writing outcomes as highlighted by national assessments. The technical challenges lie in fine-tuning and prompt engineering Large Language Models (LLMs) to accurately evaluate and provide constructive feedback on creative writing across diverse ELA activities, age groups, and proficiency levels. The research objectives include developing and validating proprietary AI algorithms aligned to the unique literacy fluency, comprehension, and creativity-based project while ensuring data integrity and privacy and conducting field data collection and usability studies. The anticipated technical results include a robust AI feedback system capable of providing real-time, personalized feedback that fosters both creativity and literacy skills, thereby enhancing ELA education through improved literacy rates and improving long-term student outcomes. The primary technical risks stem from fine-tuning and prompt engineering challenges unique to maintaining educationally valid and reliable outcomes, to ensure model effectiveness across varying ELA standards, age groups, and proficiency levels. These risks will be mitigated through extensive research, iterative development, and rigorous evaluation to ensure the AI model's efficacy and reliability.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
SBIR Phase I: AI-Enhanced Feedback to Accelerate Literacy, Creativity, and Student Engagement

Award Number: 2507435 

This National Science Foundation Small Business Innovation Research Phase I project developed and tested AI Feedback for Creativity (AIFC), a capability within the Inspire Reading platform designed to support reading, writing, and creative thinking for students in grades 3–8. The project addressed a common classroom challenge: teachers need time to provide individualized feedback on open-ended student work. AIFC explored whether artificial intelligence could provide timely, useful feedback while keeping educators responsible for instructional decisions.

During the award, the team built a working browser-based prototype that connected reading activities, student responses, AI scoring, personalized feedback, and revision. Learning activities encouraged students to understand texts, explain their reasoning, generate original ideas, and improve their responses. Materials included passages at three reading levels, comprehension supports, and text-to-speech features to accommodate different learning needs.

The project’s principal contribution to knowledge was evidence that AI could evaluate open-ended responses consistently when guided by clear scoring criteria and educator expertise. The system used teacher-scored examples and approved instructional materials rather than searching the open web. It combined three AI scoring judgments for each assessed skill and generated feedback in a separate step. Teachers helped develop scoring criteria, prepare examples, review outputs, and guide quality improvements.

In a validation study involving four English language arts teachers, AI scores showed substantial agreement with the teachers’ consensus judgments. Agreement reached 0.77 on a statistical measure called quadratic weighted kappa, exceeding the project’s predefined target of greater than 0.70. This finding supported the technical feasibility of AI scoring guided by explicit educational criteria. It did not establish that every feedback message was equally effective or that performance was consistent across all student groups.

The prototype was implemented in 10 classes at three public-school sites in Brookline, Portland, and San Antonio. The field implementation included 193 students in grades 3–7 and produced 512 completed learning activities. Of the participating students, 167 completed at least one activity and 112 completed at least two.

Classroom results showed that students generally acted on the feedback. Across 433 analyzed before-and-after revision transitions, 97% of responses changed following feedback, and 64% became longer. These findings demonstrated that the system could operate in authentic classrooms and support a feedback-and-revision process. However, changes in response length or wording do not by themselves demonstrate improved writing quality. The project did not establish that AIFC caused gains in literacy or creative-thinking proficiency.

The project’s broader contribution was a tested approach to making individualized feedback more accessible during classroom learning. Its browser-based design required no specialized classroom hardware, and its reading-level options and accessibility supports were designed to serve students with varied needs. Educator oversight, content moderation, controlled access, and records supporting review were incorporated into the prototype.

The award produced functioning software, instructional materials, scoring criteria, a curated collection of examples, and classroom evidence that provide a foundation for further research. Priorities identified include controlled studies of learning outcomes, evaluation of fairness across student groups, assessment of feedback quality, and improvements in cost and responsiveness at larger scale. Phase I established technical feasibility and student use of feedback while defining the evidence still needed to demonstrate lasting educational benefits .
